vignette:
Ravi was a 26-year-old South Asian man who had been married less than a year and worked as an editor, often late into the evening in a quiet office where he could lose himself in copy and avoid being alone with his thoughts. His symptoms began after a police encounter in his early twenties, when he was stopped, questioned for hours, and manhandled in a holding room that smelled of sweat, disinfectant, and stale metal. He remembered standing with his wrists twisted behind him in a position that left his shoulders aching, the harsh air on his skin, and the helplessness of being surrounded by officers who treated his fear as insolence. What had made that night stick was not only the humiliation but the sense that he had no way to explain himself or make it stop.

In the months afterward, certain moments in ordinary life began to feel loaded with danger. If his skin was suddenly hit by a particular temperature—cold air from a fan, a chill surface in a room, even a splash of water he had not expected—Ravi would go tight inside and immediately judge himself for falling apart over something so small. He had come to believe his reactions since the event showed that he was a lousy coper, and that belief hardened quickly into the thought that nothing good could happen to him anymore. The same thing happened when he found himself alone with women, even in innocent situations such as chatting with a female colleague in the office hallway or being left in a room with his wife’s cousin at family gatherings; he would feel exposed and strangely watched, as if any interaction could go wrong and confirm that he was not capable of handling his own life. At work, he noticed that the sight of his editor’s desk, the office hum, and even a sudden draft across his forearms could leave him unsettled and self-critical, and he started arranging his day so he would not be caught off guard.

Once those beliefs took hold, the memories grew sharper and more intrusive. When the event came to mind, Ravi did not just remember it as a story; he felt overwhelming grief rise in his chest, and the memory seemed to pull his body back into the same position it had been in that room, shoulders pulled back, arms held awkwardly, jaw clenched. Sometimes the memory arrived with a smell he could not place for a second but knew belonged to that night, and the combination of the odor and the bodily sensation made him feel that the humiliation was happening again rather than being remembered. Afterward he would sink into the thought that nothing in his life felt meaningful anymore. He had once taken pride in his work, in sending polished pages to print and in building a home with his wife, but now those things felt thin and distant, as if the event had emptied them of value.

That grief and those memories also fed the very situations he feared most. After a vivid recollection, Ravi became more alert to temperature changes and to whether women were nearby, scanning rooms before entering them and feeling a jolt of dread if he realized he might be left alone with a woman in an office meeting or at a family visit. The moment he began to feel detached or unreal, he took that as proof that he was not in control, and the thought that he was a poor coper returned with force. He then avoided small practical risks that had become tied to the memory: he asked colleagues to keep doors open, arranged to work from home more often, and would leave social gatherings early if he thought he might be left in a one-to-one conversation with a woman. Those choices brought brief relief, but they also narrowed his life; he became less present with his wife, less willing to attend family events, and increasingly isolated in the very routines he had tried to preserve.

By the time he sought help, Ravi was tired of living in this shrinking circle. He described feeling trapped between the grief that rushed in when he remembered the night with police and the self-contempt that followed every bad moment, each feeding the other until even a cold room or a brief pause alone with a woman could set the whole sequence in motion. He came to treatment because he was afraid that if this continued, he would lose not only his confidence but the meaning he had once found in his work and marriage, and he was hoping for a way to feel like himself again without bracing for the next reminder.
